### `Hom(Complex,Matrix)`
- **Domain:** [Complex](../../Complexes/type/Complex.md), [Matrix](../../Core/type/Matrix.md)
- **Returns:** [ComplexMap](../../Complexes/type/ComplexMap.md) (this method)

> The map of complexes between Hom complexes

The maps $f: C \to D$ and $g: E \to F$ of chain complexes induces the map $h = Hom(f, g) : Hom(D, E) \to Hom(C, F)$ defined by $\phi \mapsto g \phi f$. We illustrate the defining property of the map $h$ on a random element $\phi$ in degree zero. If either of the arguments is a [Complex](../../Complexes/type/Complex.md), that argument is understood to be the identity map on that complex. If either of the arguments is a [Module](../../Core/type/Module.md) or a [Ring](../../Core/type/Ring.md), that argument is understood to be the identity map on the complex having a unique non-zero term in in homological degree 0.  The ring must be the underlying ring of the map of complexes. If either of the arguments is a [Matrix](../../Core/type/Matrix.md), that argument is understood to be a map of complexes whose source and target have a unique non-zero entry in homological degree 0. XXX write this text after writing doc for homomorphism and homomorphism'. This routine is functorial.

### `Hom(Matrix,Complex)`
- **Domain:** [Matrix](../../Core/type/Matrix.md), [Complex](../../Complexes/type/Complex.md)
- **Returns:** [ComplexMap](../../Complexes/type/ComplexMap.md) (this method)

> The map of complexes between Hom complexes

The maps $f: C \to D$ and $g: E \to F$ of chain complexes induces the map $h = Hom(f, g) : Hom(D, E) \to Hom(C, F)$ defined by $\phi \mapsto g \phi f$. We illustrate the defining property of the map $h$ on a random element $\phi$ in degree zero. If either of the arguments is a [Complex](../../Complexes/type/Complex.md), that argument is understood to be the identity map on that complex. If either of the arguments is a [Module](../../Core/type/Module.md) or a [Ring](../../Core/type/Ring.md), that argument is understood to be the identity map on the complex having a unique non-zero term in in homological degree 0.  The ring must be the underlying ring of the map of complexes. If either of the arguments is a [Matrix](../../Core/type/Matrix.md), that argument is understood to be a map of complexes whose source and target have a unique non-zero entry in homological degree 0. XXX write this text after writing doc for homomorphism and homomorphism'. This routine is functorial.

### `Hom(ComplexMap,Matrix)`
- **Domain:** [ComplexMap](../../Complexes/type/ComplexMap.md), [Matrix](../../Core/type/Matrix.md)
- **Returns:** [ComplexMap](../../Complexes/type/ComplexMap.md) (this method)

> The map of complexes between Hom complexes

The maps $f: C \to D$ and $g: E \to F$ of chain complexes induces the map $h = Hom(f, g) : Hom(D, E) \to Hom(C, F)$ defined by $\phi \mapsto g \phi f$. We illustrate the defining property of the map $h$ on a random element $\phi$ in degree zero. If either of the arguments is a [Complex](../../Complexes/type/Complex.md), that argument is understood to be the identity map on that complex. If either of the arguments is a [Module](../../Core/type/Module.md) or a [Ring](../../Core/type/Ring.md), that argument is understood to be the identity map on the complex having a unique non-zero term in in homological degree 0.  The ring must be the underlying ring of the map of complexes. If either of the arguments is a [Matrix](../../Core/type/Matrix.md), that argument is understood to be a map of complexes whose source and target have a unique non-zero entry in homological degree 0. XXX write this text after writing doc for homomorphism and homomorphism'. This routine is functorial.

### `Hom(Matrix,ComplexMap)`
- **Domain:** [Matrix](../../Core/type/Matrix.md), [ComplexMap](../../Complexes/type/ComplexMap.md)
- **Returns:** [ComplexMap](../../Complexes/type/ComplexMap.md) (this method)

> The map of complexes between Hom complexes

The maps $f: C \to D$ and $g: E \to F$ of chain complexes induces the map $h = Hom(f, g) : Hom(D, E) \to Hom(C, F)$ defined by $\phi \mapsto g \phi f$. We illustrate the defining property of the map $h$ on a random element $\phi$ in degree zero. If either of the arguments is a [Complex](../../Complexes/type/Complex.md), that argument is understood to be the identity map on that complex. If either of the arguments is a [Module](../../Core/type/Module.md) or a [Ring](../../Core/type/Ring.md), that argument is understood to be the identity map on the complex having a unique non-zero term in in homological degree 0.  The ring must be the underlying ring of the map of complexes. If either of the arguments is a [Matrix](../../Core/type/Matrix.md), that argument is understood to be a map of complexes whose source and target have a unique non-zero entry in homological degree 0. XXX write this text after writing doc for homomorphism and homomorphism'. This routine is functorial.

# HomePage
The preamble of a package

- **Package:** [Core](../../Core/package/Core.md)
- **Class:** [Symbol](../../Core/type/Symbol.md)
- **Aliases:** `Core$HomePage`

## Description
The dictionaries for the symbols in the packages loaded by the user are moved out of the way to avoid conflicts, so just the standard pre-loaded packages are visible to the source code of the package.  In addition, the package [SimpleDoc](../../SimpleDoc/package/SimpleDoc.md) is made available. If functions from additional packages are needed by the code in the new package, then [needsPackage](../../Core/methodFunction/needsPackage.md) can be used (after the use of `newPackage`) to provide them. If functions from additional packages are needed by the user who will load the new package, then [needsPackage](../../Core/methodFunction/needsPackage.md) can be used (before the use of `newPackage`) to provide them. The options can be recovered with [options](../../Core/methodFunction/options.md) as follows. Here is a template for a typical `newPackage` entry in a package.

#### Consequences
A package is created

## Examples
```macaulay2
newPackage("Foo",
Version => "1.1",
Headline => "making Foo",
Configuration => { "foo" => 42, "bar" => "x" }
)
```

```
o1 = Foo
o1 : Package
```

```macaulay2
endPackage "Foo"
```

```
o2 = Foo
o2 : Package
```

```macaulay2
opts = options Foo
```

```
o3 : OptionTable
```

```macaulay2
opts.Headline

```

# Homogenization
Algorithm for computing free resolutions by first homogenizing

- **Package:** [Complexes](../../Complexes/package/Complexes.md)
- **Class:** [Symbol](../../Core/type/Symbol.md)
- **Aliases:** `Complexes$Homogenization`

## Description
This is one of the algorithms written at top level of Macaulay2 for computing free resolutions, although it uses engine code to compute free resolutions of the homogenized module or ideal.  This is the default strategy for inhomogeneous ideals or modules over a commutative ring. The result is rarely a minimal resolution; minimal resolutions are not generally defined in the inhomogeneous case. This first example computes a free resolution of an inhomogeneous ideal. Even though minimal resolutions are not generally defined, the [minimize(Complex)](minimize_lpar_Complex_rpar_.md) method will often produce a smaller resolution. When the input is an ideal $I$, the free resolution of $S^1/I$ is returned. This strategy also works over quotient rings. This strategy homogenizes the ideal or module as well as the underlying ring, calls an engine routine to compute the resolution, and finally dehomogenizes the result.

name: ImmutableType

# ImmutableType
The class of all immutable types

- **Package:** [Core](../../Core/package/Core.md)
- **Class:** [Type](../../Core/type/Type.md)
- **Parent:** [HashTable](../../Core/type/HashTable.md)
- **Aliases:** `Core$ImmutableType`

## Description
All types are implemented as hash tables.  Most types are mutable, so that additional methods for handling their instances can be added at any time.  However, if a type has an ancestor where the methods can be stored, then mutability is not needed. When a type is used to represent a mathematical object, then immutability is desirable, in order to make the strict equality operator work on it.  For example, a module `M` is a type, with its elements are its instances, but we would like to be able to compare two modules quickly, and form sets of modules.  This is possible, because we have implemented modules as immutable types, and we have put the methods for adding and subtracting elements of `M` into the class [Vector](../../Core/type/Vector.md). Another advantage of immutability of modules is that there is no particular reason, aside from efficiency, to avoid creating a given module multiple times, as one copy of the module is as good as another.

# Increment
Find a primary component corresponding to an associated prime

- **Package:** [PrimaryDecomposition](../../PrimaryDecomposition/package/PrimaryDecomposition.md)
- **Class:** [Symbol](../../Core/type/Symbol.md)
- **Aliases:** `PrimaryDecomposition$Increment`
- **Examples:** _undocumented_

## Description
The output `Q` is `topComponents(I + P^m)` for sufficiently large `m`. The criterion that `Q` is primary is given in Eisenbud-Huneke-Vasconcelos, Invent. Math. 110 (1992) 207-235. However, we use [localize(Ideal,Ideal)](localize_lpar_Ideal_cma_Ideal_rpar_.md). The `Strategy` option value sets the strategy option for [localize](../../PrimaryDecomposition/methodFunction/localize.md), and should be one of the following: Strategy => 0 -- Uses `localize` Strategy 0Strategy => 1 -- Uses `localize` Strategy 1Strategy => 2 -- Uses `localize` Strategy 2The `Increment` option value should be an integer. The algorithm given in Eisenbud-Huneke-Vasconcelos, Invent. Math. 110 (1992) 207-235, relies on `topComponents(I + P^m)` for $m$ sufficiently large. The algorithm begins with $m = 1$, and increases $m$ by the value of the `Increment` option until `m` is sufficiently large. The default value is 1. Authored by [C. Yackel](http://faculty.mercer.edu/yackel_ca). Last modified June, 2000.

## Source
```m2
primaryComponent = method( Options => { Strategy => 2, Increment => 1 })
```

name: Indent

# Indent
Encode Macaulay2 things as JSON data

- **Package:** [JSON](../../JSON/package/JSON.md)
- **Class:** [Symbol](../../Core/type/Symbol.md)
- **Aliases:** `JSON$Indent`
- **See also:** _undocumented_

## Description
This method (which is also available using its synonym `json`) returns a string containing JSON data corresponding to the given Macaulay2 thing.  If the `Indent` option is `null` (the default), then there are no newlines or indentation. If the `Indent` option is an integer, then newlines are added between values of arrays and members of lists and the given integer determines the number of spaces to indent for each level of indentation. Alternatively, the `Indent` option can be a string corresponding to the indentation used for each level. The `ValueSeparator` option determines the string to use between values in an array and members in an object.  If it is `null` (the default), then the string will either be `", "` or `","`, depending on whether `Indent` is `null` or not, respectively. Otherwise, the given string is used. The `NameSeparator` option determines the string to use after the name of an object member.  By default, it is `": "`. By default, the members of objects are given in arbitrary order.  To sort them by name in lexicographic order as strings, use the `Sort` option.

## Examples
```macaulay2
x = hashTable {"foo" => {1, 2, {pi, true, false, null}}}
```

```
o1 = HashTable{"foo" => {1, 2, {pi, true, false, }}}
o1 : HashTable
```

```macaulay2
toJSON x
```

# IndexedVariable
The class of all indexed variables

- **Package:** [Core](../../Core/package/Core.md)
- **Class:** [Type](../../Core/type/Type.md)
- **Parent:** [BasicList](../../Core/type/BasicList.md)
- **Aliases:** `Core$IndexedVariable`
- **See also:** _undocumented_

## Description
Indexed variables provide the possibility of producing polynomial rings `R[x_0, x_1, ..., x_(n-1)]` in n variables, where n is not known in advance.  If `x` is an symbol, and i is an integer, then `x_i` produces an indexed variable. After this has been done, an assignment `x_i=v` will assign another value to it.  A new sequence of indexed variables of length n assigned to the symbol `x` can be produced with `x_1 .. x_n` and that sequence can be used in constructing a polynomial ring. Warning: the values of the indexed variables `t_i` are stored in a global location, behind the scenes, so may not get garbage collected, even if `t` is a local variable.

# IntegralClosure
Routines for integral closure of affine domains and ideals

- **Package:** [IntegralClosure](../../IntegralClosure/package/IntegralClosure.md)
- **Version:** 1.10
- **Class:** [Package](../../Core/type/Package.md)
- **Aliases:** `IntegralClosure$IntegralClosure`, `Package$IntegralClosure`
- **See also:** _undocumented_

## Description
This package contains several algorithms for computing the integral closure (i.e. normalization) of an affine domain, and also of an ideal. The basic use of this package is shown in the following example. Use [icFractions](../../IntegralClosure/methodFunction/icFractions.md) to see what fractions have been added. Look at the ideal of S or the generators of S to see the structure of the integral closure. The integral closure of an ideal can be computed as follows. Integral closures of powers of ideals can be computed in a more efficient manner than using e.g. `integralClosure(I^d)`, by using e.g. `integralClosure(I, d)`. If the characteristic is positive, yet small compared to the degree, but the fraction ring is still separable over a subring, then use [icFracP](../../IntegralClosure/methodFunction/icFracP.md), which is an implementation of an algorithm due to Leonard-Pellikaan, and modified by Singh-Swanson (see arXiv:0901.0871). However, the interface to this routine is likely to change in future releases to more closely match the functions above. The method used by integralClosure is a modification of the basic algorithm explained in Theo De Jong's paper An Algorithm for Computing the Integral Closure, J. Symbolic Computation, (1998) 26, 273-277.### AuthorsFor the programmerThe object [IntegralClosure](../../IntegralClosure/package/IntegralClosure.md) is a [Package](../../Core/type/Package.md), defined in `IntegralClosure.m2`, with auxiliary files in `IntegralClosure/`.

## Authors

# InternalDegree
A random map of chain complexes

- **Package:** [Complexes](../../Complexes/package/Complexes.md)
- **Class:** [Symbol](../../Core/type/Symbol.md)
- **Aliases:** `Complexes$InternalDegree`

## Description
A random complex map $f: C \to D$ is obtained from a random element in the complex [Hom(Complex,Complex)](Hom_lpar_Complex_cma_Complex_rpar_.md). When the random element in the complex $Hom(C, D)$ lies in the kernel of the differential, the associated map of complexes commutes with the differential. When the random element in the complex $Hom(C, D)$ lies in the image of the differential, the associated map of complexes is a null homotopy. When the degree of the random element in the complex $Hom(C, D)$ is non-zero, the associated map of complexes has the same degree. By default, the random element is constructed as a random linear combination of the basis elements in the appropriate degree of $Hom(C, D)$.  Given an internal degree, the random element is constructed as maps of modules with this degree.

# InverseSystems
Macaulay's Inverse Systems

- **Package:** [InverseSystems](../../InverseSystems/package/InverseSystems.md)
- **Version:** 1.1
- **Class:** [Package](../../Core/type/Package.md)
- **Aliases:** `InverseSystems$InverseSystems`, `Package$InverseSystems`

## Description
Inverse systems are often used to construct artinian Gorenstein ideals and modules. For a brief introduction to that application, see [Gorenstein](../../InverseSystems/symbol/Gorenstein.md). Here we give a general introduction. The graded Hopf algebra dual of the symmetric algebra $S:= k[x_1,\dots, x_n]$ is the divided power algebra $D$. The dual basis to the monomial basis of $S$ is the basis consisting of monomials of the form $x_1^{(m_1)} \dots x_n^{(m_n)}$. In characteristic zero, $S$ and $D$ are isomorphic as algebras, with isomorphism sending $x_i^{a}$ to $a!x_i^{(a)}$. In general the multiplication in $D$ is defined by the same formulas as in characteristic 0. For example,$x_1^{(1)}*x_1^{(1)} = 2*x_1^{(2)}$. In positive characteristic $D$ and $S$ are not isomorphic; $D$ is not even a finitely generated algebra. We will be interested also in the local versions, where we take power series in the divided powers. This is the ordinary linear dual of $S$. We denote it by $D'$. As an $S$-module, $D'$ is the injective hull of the simple module $S/(x_1,\dots, x_n)$. Since $D$ is the graded dual of $S$, it may also be regarded as an $S$-module. Any element of $D$ is annihilated by a power of $mm = (x_1,\dots, x_n)$, so the action of $S$ on $D$ or $D'$ extends to an action of the power series ring k[[x_1,\dots, x_n]]. F. S. Macaulay defined the inverse system of an $S'$-submodule M of $D'$ to be the annihilator I of M in $S'$ (or in $S$).  If $M$ is finitely generated then it is annihilated by some power of $mm$, and thus I is 0-dimensional. Inversely, the (local) inverse system of an ideal in $S$ or $S'$ is by definition the submodule of $D'$ that it annihilates. In the 1880's these ideas were used by Max Noether, in the local version, as a substitute for primary decomposition in the case of what he called multiple points in the plane. F. S. Macaulay studied and greatly refined Noether's work, and for example identified the ideals I that are annihilators of cyclic submodules of $D'$ as the ideals such that one could do residuation in $S'/I$ -- that is, $S'/I$ is Gorenstein. Though the global version has also been studied, we will only be concerned with the local version. Any finitely generated submodule of D' generated by finite polynomials is actually a submodule of D, and its dual will have only primary components contained in $(x_1,\dots, x_n)$ so the distinction will not be important for us on that side. However, it is important to note that when taking the inverse system of an ideal, only the primary components contained in $(x_1,\dots, x_n)$ play a role.%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%Going from a submodule of D to an ideal of S (or from a submodule of D^r to a submodule of S^r: Because D and D' are not finitely generated S-modules Macaulay2 cannot deal with them directly. These scripts can only deal with a finitely generated submodule M of D or D'. Such a module is represented here by a row matrix, of ordinary polynomials, whose entries are thought of as generators of M. More generally, we represent a finitely generated submodule of $D^r$ as an $r$-rowed matrix M of ordinary polynomials. In the default behavior of the scriptinverseSystem M = inverseSystem(M, DividedPowers => false)a monomial $x^a$ is taken to represent $a!x^{(a)} \in D'$, where, if $a = (a_1,\dots, a_n)$, then $a! = a_1!*\dots*a_n!$. This means that the script should not be used in the default way unless the characteristic is greater than the highest degree to which a variable appears. To make $x^a$ represent $x^{(a)}$, for example in small characteristics, useinverseSystem(Matrix, DividedPowers=>true)(which was and remains the default behavior of the script "fromDual"). The reason for the default choice is that the general linear group GL_n(k) acts on both S and D, and it is reasonable to expect that the operations defined by inverseSystem should be equivariant. This is the case for the default setting, but with DividedPowers=>true it is not the case. For example, differs only by a linear change of coordinates from the idealBut is has very different properties than the idealWith the default behavior (DividedPowers=>false), inverseSystem is equivariant in a precise sense: If G is an $n\times n$ invertible scalar matrix, then G defines an automorphism g: S\to S by change of variables. Also g also acts on 1 x m matrices M, componentwise and (transpose g)^{-1} (inverseSystem M) = inverseSystem(g M), as illustrated below: These may look different, but... Equivalently, There is a similar equivariance for the dual action of inverseSystem on ideals.%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%Going from an ideal of S to a submodule of D, or from a submodule of S^r to a submodule of D^r. If $I$ is an ideal of $S$, homogeneous or not, we regard $I$ as an ideal of $S'$, and similarly with submodules of S^n. In either case we allow the function to accept either a submodule or its matrix of generators (a matrix with target S^n, possibly with generators in different degrees. If I is an ideal or a submodule, then M = inverseSystem(d, I) M1 = inverseSystem(d, I, DividedPowers => true)both return 1 x m matrices whose entries are the minimal generators of the annihilator of $I$ in $D'$, correct up to degree d. In the matrix $M$ a term $x^a$ is to be interpreted as $a! x^{(a)}$, while in the matrix $M1$ it is interpreted as $x^{(a)}$. Of course the first computation is only valid if all the powers of variables appearing in the generators of $I$ are < char k.%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%5 The functor inverseSystem ( -- ) and inverseSystem (d,-- ) are inverse contravariant isomorphisms between the categories of bounded length submodules of D^r and bounded co-length submodules of S^r (the bound depends on d in an obvious way.)but with a smaller value of d this would not work: There is at present no direct way to compare inverseSystem(d, inverseSystem M) and M, since the matrices representing these submodules are really representing sets of generators in D^r. However, we can check equality of containment by applying inverseSystem again:%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%% Method: To represent finitely generated S-submodule of $D'$ as an S-module we use the map of modules S/(x_1^d,\dots, x_n^d) -> D' sending $x^a$ to contract(x^a, product(1 .. n, i -> x_i^(d-1))), and its inverse, which is of course defined only on divided monomials of small degree.

#### Caveat
The translations used involve multiplying or dividing by scalars; if the polynomials involved have maximum degree n, then n! must be invertible for theUsing the tool of translation to make sense.### AuthorsFor the programmerThe object [InverseSystems](../../InverseSystems/package/InverseSystems.md) is a [Package](../../Core/type/Package.md), defined in `InverseSystems.m2`.

# Iterator
Class for iterators

- **Package:** [Core](../../Core/package/Core.md)
- **Class:** [SelfInitializingType](../../Core/type/SelfInitializingType.md)
- **Parent:** [FunctionClosure](../../Core/type/FunctionClosure.md)
- **Aliases:** `Core$Iterator`
- **See also:** _undocumented_

## Description
This is a class designed to simplify writing [iterator](../../Core/methodFunction/iterator.md) methods. Each instance is a nullary [FunctionClosure](../../Core/type/FunctionClosure.md) that serves as the [next](../../Core/methodFunction/next.md) method for the iterator. Each call of `next iter` is equivalent to `iter()`. Every `Iterator` object is an iterator for itself. However, we cannot "rewind" an `Iterator` object.  Every time that it is iterated upon using [for](../../Core/symbol/for.md), [scan](../../Core/function/scan.md), etc., iteration will resume where it left off previously. Contrast this with most other classes with the [iterator](../../Core/methodFunction/iterator.md) method installed, like, strings, for which a new `Iterator` object is created every time it is iterated upon, and so iteration starts over from the beginning

# Key
Key of a documentation node

- **Package:** [Core](../../Core/package/Core.md)
- **Class:** [Symbol](../../Core/type/Symbol.md)
- **Aliases:** `Core$Key`
- **Examples:** _undocumented_

## Description
The document key is the name of the node, specifically the one that allows users to find the documentation for the desired command. Some node names, rather than being strings, are sequences of Macaulay2 objects that refer to specific method functions. If one is documenting a function of Macaulay2, the key will just be the function's name, as in the documentation for [resolution](resolution.md). However, if one is documenting a method for a function, then the key will have a different form, as in the documentation for [resolution(Module)](resolution_lpar_Module_rpar_.md). If one is documenting an optional argument to a function, then the key has a different form still, as in [resolution(...,SyzygyLimit=>...)](resolution_lpar__dot__dot__dot__cma_SyzygyLimit_eq__gt__dot__dot__dot__rpar_.md). Finally, if one is documenting an overview of a group of functions or a package, as in [ideals](ideals.md) then one would set up a document key of the form:

#### Caveat
No two documentation nodes may have the same key or even a key that is a synonym for a key which is already used. However, sometimes there is a need for several documentation nodes to have the same key. This happens when a command that needs to be documented is a synonym for another already documented command. In this case the synonym's key should be stated in quotation marks. As an example, look at the documentation for [SUBSECTION](SUBSECTION.md) and [HEADER2](../../Text/type/HEADER2.md) in [Text.m2](common/share/Macaulay2/Text.m2).

#### Consequences
Specifies the name under which the documentation is stored

## Source

```m2
	if instance(tag.Key, Symbol) then toString tag.Key else tag.Key, tag.Format, tag.Package})
```

# LLL
Compute an LLL basis

- **Package:** [LLLBases](../../LLLBases/package/LLLBases.md)
- **Class:** [MethodFunctionWithOptions](../../Core/type/MethodFunctionWithOptions.md)
- **Aliases:** `LLLBases$LLL`

## Description
This function is provided by the package [LLLBases](../../LLLBases/package/LLLBases.md).  If the optional argument `ChangeMatrix=>true` is given, then the output is a pair of matrices: the first is the LLL matrix as above, and the second is the change of basis matrix from the original basis to the new basis. In this example, we compute the LLL basis of the nullspace of a matrix.  This is an example of Havas et al. It is also possible to get the change of basis matrix from the original basis to the LLL basis.  For example,

#### Caveat
If the strategy given is not an NTL strategy, then the columns of the matrix m must be linearly independent. In any case, the matrix must be defined over the ring ZZ.

## Parameters
- **m** — a [Matrix](../../Core/type/Matrix.md), or a "MutableMatrix", over "ZZ", whose columns are linearly independent

## Returns
A matrix or mutable matrix, respectively, whose columns form an LLL (Lenstra-Lenstra-Lovasz) basis of the image lattice of the matrix

## Options
- **[Threshold](../../LLLBases/symbol/Threshold.md)**
- **[ChangeMatrix](../../Core/symbol/ChangeMatrix.md)** — also find change of basis matrix (default: `false`)
- **[Limit](../../Core/symbol/Limit.md)** (default: `infinity`)
- **[Strategy](../../Core/symbol/Strategy.md)** — choose among different algorithms (default: `NTL`)

## Methods

- [`LLL(MutableMatrix)`](#lllmutablematrix)

# LLLBases
Lattice reduction (Lenstra-Lenstra-Lovasz bases)

- **Package:** [LLLBases](../../LLLBases/package/LLLBases.md)

- **Aliases:** `LLLBases$LLLBases`, `Package$LLLBases`

## Description
LLLBases is a package implementing several variants of LLL bases. Some of these are implemented in the Macaulay2 engine, some by Victor Shoup's NTL package, and some are implemented at top level. A matrix over ZZ determines a lattice: this is the ZZ-module generated by the columns.  It also determines a generating set. See the book: [H. Cohen, ...] for the definition and the basic algorithms for computing LLL bases. LLL bases have nice theoretical properties, but the main benefit of LLL bases is that the entries of the resulting matrix often have dramatically small size, even smaller than theory would imply. # LUdecomposition
Compute the LU decomposition of a matrix

- **Package:** [Core](../../Core/package/Core.md)
- **Class:** [MethodFunction](../../Core/type/MethodFunction.md)
- **Aliases:** `Core$LUdecomposition`

## Description
The output matrices are mutable exactly when the input matrix is, but the matrix `A` is not modifiedIf `Q` is the `m` by `m` permutation matrix such that `Q_(P_i, i) = 1`, and all other entries are zero, then `A = QLU`. There are several restrictions.  The first is that there are only a limited number of rings for which this function is implemented. Second, if `A` is a mutable matrix  defined over `RR` or `CC`, then `A` must be densely encoded.  This restriction is not present if `A` is a [Matrix](../../Core/type/Matrix.md). For matrices over `RR` or `CC`, this function calls the LAPACK routines, which are restricted to 53 bits of precision. Mutable matrices can sometimes be useful for speed, and/or space. If `A` is a mutable matrix, it must be densely encoded (which is the default).

#### Caveat
This function is limited in scope, but is sometimes useful for very large matrices

## Parameters
- **A** — a [MutableMatrix](../../Core/type/MutableMatrix.md), or a [Matrix](../../Core/type/Matrix.md),of size m by n, over a a finite field ZZ/p, "RR" or "CC"

## Returns
P, a [List](../../Core/type/List.md), of integers in [0, ..., m-1] forming a permutation; L, a [MutableMatrix](../../Core/type/MutableMatrix.md), or a [Matrix](../../Core/type/Matrix.md), an m by min(m,n) lower triangular matrix, with 1's on the diagonal; U, a [MutableMatrix](../../Core/type/MutableMatrix.md), or a [Matrix](../../Core/type/Matrix.md), a min(m,n) by n upper triangular matrix

- [`LUdecomposition(Matrix)`](#ludecompositionmatrix)

# Layout
Relative locations of Macaulay2 files

- **Package:** [Core](../../Core/package/Core.md)
- **Class:** [HashTable](../../Core/type/HashTable.md)
- **Aliases:** `Core$Layout`

## Description
Macaulay2 comes with a variety of types of files, and some of them are associated with a particular Macaulay2 package.  The hash table `currentLayout` is a translation table from names, corresponding to the various types of files, to directory paths.  The directory paths are to be interpreted relative to the path stored in [prefixDirectory](../../Core/object/prefixDirectory.md).  Each of the directories contained in the list [prefixPath](../../Core/object/prefixPath.md) has its own layout, which will be detected at runtime. Some of the strings contain `PKG` as a substring, which should be replaced by the name of package whose files will be stored in that directory. The hash table [Layout](../../Core/table/Layout.md) contains the two possible values for [currentLayout](../../Core/table/currentLayout.md); corresponding to the two possible values for the [installPackage(...,SeparateExec=>...)](installPackage_lpar__dot__dot__dot__cma_SeparateExec_eq__gt__dot__dot__dot__rpar_.md) option used with [installPackage](../../Core/methodFunction/installPackage.md). The hash table `Layout#2` is used if architecture dependent files are to be stored in a directory tree separate from the one used for architecture independent files.  The hash table `Layout#1` is used otherwise. Basic Macaulay2 files are regarded as being associated with a special package called `Core`, and the corresponding documentation files are part of the package `Macaulay2Doc`. Here are the meanings of the keys used in [currentLayout](../../Core/table/currentLayout.md).`"bin"` : executable files (M2)`"data"` : architecture independent data files`"docdir"` : documentation for Macaulay2 packages`"emacs"` : Emacs source files (*.el, *.elc)`"factory gftables"` : directory for files containing addition tables in small finite fields used by the library 'factory'`"info"` : documentation in info form`"lib"` : architecture dependent data and executable files`"libraries"` : dynamically loadable libraries from third party packages linked with Macaulay2`"man"` : man pages`"package"` : additional source files for the Macaulay2 package PKG`"packagecache"` : cached data files for the Macaulay2 package PKG`"packagedoc"` : documentation for the Macaulay2 package PKG`"packageexampleoutput"` : example output files for the Macaulay2 package PKG`"packagehtml"` : html documentation for the Macaulay2 package PKG (*.html)`"packagelib"` : architecture dependent files for the Macaulay2 package PKG`"packages"` : source files for Macaulay2 packages; this directory appears on the path`"program licenses"` : licenses for programs to be run by Macaulay2`"programs"` : programs to be run by Macaulay2

name: Lex
markdown:
# Lex
Lexicographical monomial ordering

- **Package:** [Core](../../Core/package/Core.md)
- **Class:** [Symbol](../../Core/type/Symbol.md)
- **Aliases:** `Core$Lex`

## Description
The lexicographic order is defined by: $x^A > x^B$ if the FIRST non-zero entry of the vector of integers `A-B` is POSITIVE. The largest possible exponent of variables in `Lex` order is 2^31-1.  For efficiency reasons, the size of the exponents of variables may be restricted.  Then instead of `Lex`, one can use ` MonomialSize=>16`, which allows maximal exponent 2^15-1, or `MonomialSize=>8`, which allows maximal exponent 2^7-1. Any of these versions of `Lex` order may be combined, for example, with a weight order given by a weight vector: x^A > x^B if weight(x^A) > weight(x^B) or if weight(x^A) = weight(x^B) and if the FIRST non-zero entry of the vector of integers A-B is POSITIVE.

## Examples
```macaulay2
R = QQ[a..d, MonomialOrder => Lex];
```

```macaulay2
a^3 + a^2*b^2 + b*c
3    2 2
```

```
o2 = a  + a b  + b*c
o2 : R
```

```macaulay2
B = QQ[a..d,MonomialOrder=>Lex,MonomialSize=>16];
```

```macaulay2
a^(2^15-1)
32767
```

```
o4 = a
o4 : B
```

```macaulay2
C = QQ[a..d,MonomialOrder=>Lex,MonomialSize=>8];
```

```macaulay2
try a^(2^15-1) else "failed"
```

```
o6 = failed
```

```macaulay2
a^(2^7-1)
127
```

```
o7 = a
o7 : C
```

```macaulay2
B = QQ[a..d,MonomialSize=>16,MonomialOrder=>{Weights => {1,2,3,4}, Lex}];
```

```macaulay2
a^2 + b+ c + b*d
2
```

```
o9 = b*d + c + a  + b
o9 : B
```

## Description
Lists in Macaulay2 consist of elements of any type, enclosed in braces, and separated by commas. The length of a list has two notations, the version with the `#` is faster when writing programs. The first entry of the list has index 0.  Indexing is performed using [#](../../Core/operator/_hash_.md). Lists in Macaulay2 are immutable. See [MutableList](../../Core/type/MutableList.md) for making and using lists that you may modify. To convert lists to and from other types of [BasicList](../../Core/type/BasicList.md), in addition to [toList](../../Core/methodFunction/toList.md), one may use [new](../../Core/symbol/new.md). # LocalDictionary
The class of all local dictionaries

- **Package:** [Core](../../Core/package/Core.md)
- **Class:** [Type](../../Core/type/Type.md)
- **Parent:** [Dictionary](../../Core/type/Dictionary.md)
- **Aliases:** `Core$LocalDictionary`
- **Examples:** _undocumented_

## Description
A local dictionary is one used in connection with a local scope, such as one that is bounded by the body of a function closure. A local dictionary is created on the fly by the interpreter, and after the scope has been closed, the dictionary can be enlarged no further. Accessing local dictionaries can be a useful debugging tool.  The local dictionaries accessible to the user come with frames, so their symbols have values; thus they may be referred to as dictionary closures.

`LongPolynomial` -- a strategy used with the keyword [Strategy](../../Core/symbol/Strategy.md). Indicates that during computation of a Gröbner basis, the reduction routine will be replaced by one that will handle long polynomials more efficiently using "geobuckets", which accommodate the terms in buckets of geometrically increasing length. markdown:
# Matrix
The class of all matrices

- **Package:** [Core](../../Core/package/Core.md)
- **Class:** [Type](../../Core/type/Type.md)
- **Parent:** [HashTable](../../Core/type/HashTable.md)
- **Aliases:** `Core$Matrix`
- **Examples:** _undocumented_

## Description
A matrix is a homomorphism between two modules, together with an integer (or vector of integers) called its degree, which is used when determining whether the map is homogeneous.  The matrix is stored in the usual way as a rectangular array of ring elements. When the source or target modules are not free, the matrix is interpreted as a linear transformation in terms of the generators of the modules. A matrix `f` is an immutable object, so if you want to cache information about it, put it in the hash table `f.cache`. # MatrixExpression
The class of all matrix expressions

- **Package:** [Core](../../Core/package/Core.md)
- **Class:** [HeaderType](../../Core/type/HeaderType.md)
- **Parent:** [Expression](../../Core/type/Expression.md)
- **Aliases:** `Core$MatrixExpression`

## Description
`MatrixExpression` is a type of [Expression](../../Core/type/Expression.md) representing a matrix.

## Ancestors
- [BasicList](../../Core/type/BasicList.md)
- [Thing](../../Core/type/Thing.md)

## Common operations
- [mathML](../../Core/methodFunction/mathML.md)
- [net](../../Core/methodFunction/net.md)
- [texMath](../../Core/methodFunction/texMath.md)

## Examples
```macaulay2
MatrixExpression {{a,b,c},{a,bb,ccc}}
```

```
o1 = | a b  c   |
| a bb ccc |
o1 : Expression of class MatrixExpression
```

```macaulay2
R=QQ[x,y];
```

```macaulay2
MatrixExpression append(applyTable({{x^2-y^2,x^3-y^3},{x^2-4*y^2,x^3+y^3}},factor),Degrees=>{{{-2},{-3}},{{0},{0}}})
```

```
o3 = {-2} | (x-y)(x+y)   (x-y)(x2+xy+y2) |
{-3} | (x-2y)(x+2y) (x+y)(x2-xy+y2) |
o3 : Expression of class MatrixExpression
```

```macaulay2
value oo
```

```
o4 = {-2} | x2-y2  x3-y3 |
{-3} | x2-4y2 x3+y3 |
2      2
o4 : Matrix R  <-- R
```

# MinimalGenerators
Whether to compute minimal generators and return a trimmed set of generators

- **Package:** [Core](../../Core/package/Core.md)
- **Class:** [Symbol](../../Core/type/Symbol.md)
- **Aliases:** `Core$MinimalGenerators`

## Description
The following returns two minimal generators (Serre's Theorem: a codim 2 Gorenstein ideal is a complete intersection.)Without trimming we would get 4 generators instead. Sometimes the extra time to find the minimal generators is too large. This allows one to bypass this part of the computation.

## Examples
```macaulay2
S = ZZ/101[a,b]
```

```
o1 = S
o1 : PolynomialRing
```

```macaulay2
i = ideal(a^4,b^4)
4   4
```

```
o2 = ideal (a , b )
o2 : Ideal of S
```

```macaulay2
quotient(i, a^3+b^3)
3    3
```

```
o3 = ideal (a*b, a  - b )
o3 : Ideal of S
```

```macaulay2
quotient(i, a^3+b^3, MinimalGenerators => false)
3    3
```

```
o4 = ideal (a*b, a  - b )
o4 : Ideal of S
```

```macaulay2
needsPackage "Truncations"
```

```
o5 = Truncations
o5 : Package
```

```macaulay2
R = ZZ/101[x_0..x_4]
```

```
o6 = R
o6 : PolynomialRing
```

```macaulay2
I = monomialCurveIdeal(R, {1,4,5,9});
```

```
o7 : Ideal of R
```

```macaulay2
time J = truncate(8, I, MinimalGenerators => false);
-- used 0.00367712s (cpu); 0.00367348s (thread); 0s (gc)
```

```
o8 : Ideal of R
```

```macaulay2
time K = truncate(8, I, MinimalGenerators => true);
-- used 0.0345657s (cpu); 0.0345747s (thread); 0s (gc)
```

```
o9 : Ideal of R
```

```macaulay2
numgens J
```

```
o10 = 1067
```

```macaulay2
numgens K
```

```
o11 = 428
```

## Source
```m2
	  MinimalGenerators => true,
```

# MinimalPrimes
Minimal primes and radical routines for ideals

- **Package:** [MinimalPrimes](../../MinimalPrimes/package/MinimalPrimes.md)
- **Version:** 0.10
- **Class:** [Package](../../Core/type/Package.md)
- **Aliases:** `MinimalPrimes$MinimalPrimes`, `Package$MinimalPrimes`
- **Examples:** _undocumented_
- **See also:** _undocumented_

## Description
Find the [minimal primes of an ideal](minimal_spc_primes_spc_of_spc_an_spc_ideal.md) in a polynomial ring over a prime field, or a quotient ring of that. These are the geometric components of the corresponding algebraic set. Multiple strategies are implemented via [using hooks](using_spc_hooks.md). In many cases the default `Birational` strategy is much faster, although there are cases when the `Legacy` strategy does better. For a [MonomialIdeal](../../Core/type/MonomialIdeal.md), a more efficient algorithm is used instead.`minprimes` and `decompose` are synonyms for [minimalPrimes](../../MinimalPrimes/methodFunction/minimalPrimes.md).

#### Caveat
Only works for ideals in (commutative) polynomial rings or quotients of polynomial rings over a prime field, might have bugs in small characteristic and larger degree (although, many of these cases are caught correctly).### AuthorsFor the programmerThe object [MinimalPrimes](../../MinimalPrimes/package/MinimalPrimes.md) is a [Package](../../Core/type/Package.md), defined in `MinimalPrimes.m2`, with auxiliary files in `MinimalPrimes/`.

- Mahrud Sayrafi

name: MonomialOrder
markdown:
# MonomialOrder
Monomial ordering

- **Package:** [Core](../../Core/package/Core.md)
- **Class:** [Symbol](../../Core/type/Symbol.md)
- **Aliases:** `Core$MonomialOrder`

## Description
`MonomialOrder` -- an optional argument used with polynomial rings and monoids to indicate a monomial ordering other than the default (graded reverse lexicographic). In Macaulay2, each polynomial ring (and also each monoid) is equipped with a monomial order, which is used for display of polynomials (terms are listed in descending monomial order), and also for Gröbner basis computations. In the most general setting, a monomial ordering is given by a list of ordering tests, of various types listed and described below, each of which provides a partial ordering on the monomials.  The ordering tests are applied sequentially, starting with the first one, until one monomial is judged greater than the other. At the end, if necessary, the graded reverse lexicographic order is used to compare the monomials. For examples, see below, or see [monomial orderings](monomial_spc_orderings.md). Permissible elements:[GRevLex](../../Core/symbol/GRevLex.md) => n -- A graded reverse lexicographic block of variables[Lex](../../Core/symbol/Lex.md) => n[Weights](../../Core/symbol/Weights.md) => {...}[Position](../../Core/symbol/Position.md) => Up  or  Position => Down[RevLex](../../Core/symbol/RevLex.md) => n[GroupLex](../../Core/symbol/GroupLex.md) => n[GroupRevLex](../../Core/symbol/GroupRevLex.md) => n[MonomialSize](../../Core/symbol/MonomialSize.md) => n, n being 8,16,32, or 64.  Set the packing size for exponents for further variablesSome examples of monomial orders.  Note that if only one item is in the list, we can dispense with the list.`MonomialOrder => {GRevLex=>2, GRevLex=>3}` -- a product order`MonomialOrder => {2, 3}` -- same`MonomialOrder => {Weights=>{1,13,6,2}}` -- a weight order`MonomialOrder => Weights=>{1,13,6,2}` -- sameIf any monomials will be less than 1 in the ordering, then the option `Global => false` should be used.

## Examples
```macaulay2
QQ[x,y, Weights => {-1,1}, Global => false]
```

```
o1 = QQ[x..y]
o1 : PolynomialRing
```

```macaulay2
x<1
```

```
o2 = true
```

```macaulay2
y<1
```

```
o3 = false
```

## Source
```m2
	MonomialOrder => Ascending
```

## See also
- [grevlexWeight](grevlexWeight.md)
- [monomial orderings](monomial_spc_orderings.md)
- [weightGrevlex](weightGrevlex.md)

name: MultigradedBettiTally

# MultigradedBettiTally
The class of all multigraded Betti tallies

- **Package:** [Core](../../Core/package/Core.md)
- **Class:** [Type](../../Core/type/Type.md)
- **Parent:** [BettiTally](../../Core/type/BettiTally.md)
- **Aliases:** `Core$MultigradedBettiTally`

## Description
A multigraded Betti tally is a special type of [BettiTally](../../Core/type/BettiTally.md) that is printed as a diagram of the multigraded Betti numbers. The class was created so that the method [multigraded(BettiTally)](multigraded_lpar_BettiTally_rpar_.md) could return something that both prints nicely and from which information could be extracted. The content of a multigraded Betti tally is identical to the Betti tally from which it was constructed. By default the data is presented as a table of polynomials where each column corresponds to a given homological degree appearing as the top entry and each monomial in the other entries represents the multidegree of a given summand. When [compactMatrixForm](compactMatrixForm.md) is set to `false`, the entries represent the multidegree of summands ordered by the total weight. The number of summands corresponding to a given multidegree appears to the left of the multidegree. For convenience, various operations on `BettiTally` such as direct sum ([++](../../Core/operator/_add__add_.md)), tensor product ([**](../../Core/operator/_mul__mul_.md)), [pdim](../../Core/methodFunction/pdim.md) and degree shifting (numbers in brackets or parentheses) are extended to work with multigraded Betti tables. These operations mimic the corresponding operations on chain complexes.### ContributorsThis feature was implemented by Mahrud Sayrafi based on earlier work by Gregory G. Smith.

## Ancestors
- [VirtualTally](../../Core/type/VirtualTally.md)
- [HashTable](../../Core/type/HashTable.md)
- [Thing](../../Core/type/Thing.md)

## Common operations
- [net](../../Core/methodFunction/net.md)
- [texMath](../../Core/methodFunction/texMath.md)

## Examples
```macaulay2
B = new BettiTally from {(0, {0, 0}, 0) => 1, (1, {0, 2}, 2) => 1, (1, {1, 1}, 2) => 2, (1, {2, 0}, 2) => 1, (2, {1, 2}, 3) => 2, (2, {2, 1}, 3) => 2, (3, {2, 2}, 4) => 1}
0 1 2 3
```

```
o1 = total: 1 4 4 1
0: 1 . . .
1: . 4 4 1
o1 : BettiTally
```

```macaulay2
B = multigraded B
0             1               2       3
```

```
o2 = 0: 1             .               .       .
2: . a^2+2*a*b+b^2               .       .
3: .             . 2*a^2*b+2*a*b^2       .
4: .             .               . a^2*b^2
o2 : MultigradedBettiTally
```

```macaulay2
peek B
```

```
1:{2, 0} 2:{2, 1}
```

# MutableMatrix
The class of all mutable matrices

- **Package:** [Core](../../Core/package/Core.md)
- **Class:** [Type](../../Core/type/Type.md)
- **Parent:** [HashTable](../../Core/type/HashTable.md)
- **Aliases:** `Core$MutableMatrix`
- **Examples:** _undocumented_
- **See also:** _undocumented_

## Description
A mutable matrix in Macaulay2 is a rectangular array of elements of a specific ring, whose entries can be modified. A mutable matrix is different from a [Matrix](../../Core/type/Matrix.md) in that a matrix contains degree information for the target and source of the matrix, while a mutable matrix has no such information.  Also, more operations are provided for matrices. For an overview of mutable matrices, see [mutable matrices](mutable_spc_matrices.md). Mutable matrices can either be encoded in a sparse manner (the matrix only encodes the non-zero elements), or in a dense manner (all elements are stored -- even zeros).  The distinction is an option to several of the routines that create mutable matrices ([mutableMatrix](../../Core/methodFunction/mutableMatrix.md), [mutableIdentity](../../Core/methodFunction/mutableIdentity.md)). Certain operations over RR or CC are performed using the LAPACK library and require dense encoding of matrices: [LUdecomposition](../../Core/methodFunction/LUdecomposition.md), [SVD](../../Core/methodFunction/SVD.md), [solve](../../Core/methodFunction/solve.md), [eigenvalues](../../Core/methodFunction/eigenvalues.md), [eigenvectors](../../Core/methodFunction/eigenvectors.md).row and column operations[rowAdd](../../Core/methodFunction/rowAdd.md)[rowSwap](../../Core/methodFunction/rowSwap.md)[rowPermute](../../Core/methodFunction/rowPermute.md)[rowMult](../../Core/methodFunction/rowMult.md)[columnAdd](../../Core/methodFunction/columnAdd.md)[columnSwap](../../Core/methodFunction/columnSwap.md)[columnPermute](../../Core/methodFunction/columnPermute.md)[columnMult](../../Core/methodFunction/columnMult.md)matrix arithmeticMany matrix arithmetic routines are only available for immutable matrices, not mutable matrices.  It is necessary to use [matrix](../../Core/methodFunction/matrix.md) to make an immutable matrix first.

# Mutex
The class of mutexes

- **Package:** [Core](../../Core/package/Core.md)
- **Class:** [Type](../../Core/type/Type.md)
- **Parent:** [Thing](../../Core/type/Thing.md)
- **Aliases:** `Core$Mutex`

## Description
A mutex (short for mutual exclusion) is a synchronization primitive used to prevent multiple threads from accessing shared data at the same time. It ensures that only one thread can hold the lock at a time, which helps avoid race conditions in concurrent programs. In Macaulay2, a `Mutex` object can be used to protect critical sections of code. When a thread locks a mutex, other threads attempting to lock it will wait until it is unlocked. For example, suppose multiple threads try to modify the same string. Each thread will need to get the current value of the string, make its modification, and then save the new value.  However, there is a good chance that another thread might save its updated value after another thread has fetched it but before it saved the new value.  We can see this in the code below. We likely ended up with fewer than the expected number of 10 messages. We can get around this issue by using a mutex to lock the string so that only one thread can modify it at a time. With the mutex, all 10 messages are present.

# NameSeparator
Encode Macaulay2 things as JSON data

- **Package:** [JSON](../../JSON/package/JSON.md)
- **Class:** [Symbol](../../Core/type/Symbol.md)
- **Aliases:** `JSON$NameSeparator`
- **See also:** _undocumented_

## Description
This method (which is also available using its synonym `json`) returns a string containing JSON data corresponding to the given Macaulay2 thing.  If the `Indent` option is `null` (the default), then there are no newlines or indentation. If the `Indent` option is an integer, then newlines are added between values of arrays and members of lists and the given integer determines the number of spaces to indent for each level of indentation. Alternatively, the `Indent` option can be a string corresponding to the indentation used for each level. The `ValueSeparator` option determines the string to use between values in an array and members in an object.  If it is `null` (the default), then the string will either be `", "` or `","`, depending on whether `Indent` is `null` or not, respectively. Otherwise, the given string is used. The `NameSeparator` option determines the string to use after the name of an object member.  By default, it is `": "`. By default, the members of objects are given in arbitrary order.  To sort them by name in lexicographic order as strings, use the `Sort` option.

## Examples
```macaulay2
x = hashTable {"foo" => {1, 2, {pi, true, false, null}}}
```

```
o1 = HashTable{"foo" => {1, 2, {pi, true, false, }}}
o1 : HashTable

```


```macaulay2

```

```

"foo": [
1,
2,
[
3.141592653589793,
true,
false,
null
]
]
}
```

```macaulay2
toJSON(x, Indent => "\t")
```

```
o4 = {
"foo": [
1,
2,
[
3.141592653589793,
true,
false,
null
]
]
}
```

```macaulay2

```

```
o5 = {"foo": [1 , 2 , [3.141592653589793 , true , false , null]]}
```

```macaulay2
toJSON(x, NameSeparator => " : ")
```

```

```

```macaulay2

```

# Net
The class of all nets and strings

- **Package:** [Core](../../Core/package/Core.md)
- **Class:** [Type](../../Core/type/Type.md)
- **Parent:** [Thing](../../Core/type/Thing.md)
- **Aliases:** `Core$Net`
- **Examples:** _undocumented_
- **See also:** _undocumented_

## Description
A net is a generalization of a string that is designed to facilitate two-dimensional printing on ascii terminals.  It consists of a rectangular array of characters subdivided horizontally by an imaginary baseline. Operations on nets also accept strings by interpreting a string as a rectangle of height one with the baseline just below it.  In fact, the parent of [String](../../Core/type/String.md) is [Net](../../Core/type/Net.md). Multiple nets per line can be sent to an output file with [<<](../../Core/operator/_lt__lt_.md) but care must be taken to use [endl](../../Core/function/endl.md) to end lines, for nets with new line characters embedded in them will be displayed in an unexpected way. Warning: if so many characters are written to a file that an internal buffer is filled before the line ends or first net is seen, then the buffer will be flushed, and writing a net subsequently will produce an unexpected result.

# NetFile
The class of all net files

- **Parent:** [Thing](../../Core/type/Thing.md)

## Description
This class is experimental.  Net files are intended to supplant output files eventually.  Whereas a file is a stream of bytes, or in some non-unix operating systems, a sequence of lines each of which is a sequence of bytes, a net file is a sequence of lines, each of which is a net.  Each output line is assembled by joining nets one by one.

name: Nonminimal

# Nonminimal
Algorithm for computing nonminimal free resolutions

- **Package:** [Complexes](../../Complexes/package/Complexes.md)
- **Class:** [Symbol](../../Core/type/Symbol.md)
- **Aliases:** `Complexes$Nonminimal`

## Description
This is the main the algorithm in the engine of Macaulay2 for computing nonminimal free resolutions of possibly inhomogeneous modules and ideals over a polynomial ring or exterior algebra defined over a finite field.  For homogeneous ideals and modules over such rings, this variant generally computes a non-minimal resolution much faster than engine routines that return a minimal free resolution. In particular, this algorithm is used by [minimalBetti](../../Core/methodFunction/minimalBetti.md) for faster computation of Betti tables. This first example computes part of the free resolution of the ground field over a inhomogeneous $E_8$ singularity. We also present an inhomogeneous example over a polynomial ring. We also present an example over an exterior algebra. This strategy implements an algorithm of Frank Schreyer. It first computes lead terms of all of the syzygy modules of the ideal or module, and then determines each syzygy using a linear algebra approach together with a number of optimizations.

## Method details
### `SPACE(OO,ToricDivisor)`
- **Domain:** [OO](../../Varieties/function/OO.md), [ToricDivisor](ToricDivisor.md)
- **Returns:** _undocumented_

> Make the associated rank-one reflexive sheaf

For a Weil divisor $D$ on a normal variety $X$ the associated sheaf ${\cal O}_X(D)$ is defined by $H^0(U, {\cal O}_X(D)) = \{ f \in {\mathbb C}(X)^* | (div(f)+D)|_U \geq 0 \} \cup \{0\}$. The sheaf associated to a Weil divisor is reflexive; it is equal to its bidual.  A divisor is Cartier if and only if the associated sheaf is a line bundleThe first examples show that the associated sheaves are reflexive. Two Weil divisors $D$ and $E$ are linearly equivalent if $D = E + div(f)$, for some $f \in {\mathbb C}(X)^*$. Linearly equivalent divisors produce isomorphic sheaves.

### `_(OO,NormalToricVariety)`
- **Domain:** [OO](../../Varieties/function/OO.md), [NormalToricVariety](NormalToricVariety.md)
- **Returns:** [SheafOfRings](../../Varieties/type/SheafOfRings.md) (this method)

> Make a coherent sheaf of rings

The category of coherent sheaves on a normal toric variety is equivalent to the quotient category of finitely generated modules over the total coordinate ring by the full subcategory of torsion modules with respect to the irrelevant ideal.  In particular, the total coordinate ring corresponds to the structure sheaf. For more information, see Subsection 5.3 in Cox-Little-Schenck's Toric Varieties. On [toricProjectiveSpace](toricProjectiveSpace.md), we can make the structure sheaf in a few ways.

# OrderedMonoid
The class of all ordered monoids

- **Package:** [Core](../../Core/package/Core.md)
- **Class:** [Type](../../Core/type/Type.md)
- **Parent:** [Monoid](../../Core/type/Monoid.md)
- **Aliases:** `Core$OrderedMonoid`
- **Examples:** _undocumented_

## Description
An ordered monoid is a multiplicative monoid together with an ordering of its elements. The ordering is required to be compatible with the multiplication in the sense that if x < y then x z < y z. The class of all ordered monoids is [OrderedMonoid](../../Core/type/OrderedMonoid.md). The reason for making a separate class for ordered monoids is that monoid rings can be implemented more efficiently for them - an element of the monoid ring can be stored as a sorted list, each element of which is a pair consisting of an element of the monoid and a coefficient. A free commutative ordered monoid can be created with [monoid](../../Core/methodFunction/monoid.md).

# OverField
Algorithm for computing free resolutions over a field

- **Package:** [Complexes](../../Complexes/package/Complexes.md)
- **Class:** [Symbol](../../Core/type/Symbol.md)
- **Aliases:** `Complexes$OverField`

## Description
Every module over a field is free.  Therefore a minimal free resolution is determined by choosing a basis. This is the default strategy when the underlying ring is a field, so in practice it never needs to be specified. Our first examples are over finite fields.  Notice that the most interesting feature is the augmentation map. Finding a minimal free resolution for a module over a field is equivalent to finding a [minimalPresentation(Module)](minimalPresentation_lpar_Module_rpar_.md). This also works over the rationals, number fields, and fraction fields.

# OverZZ
Algorithm for computing free resolutions of ZZ-modules

- **Package:** [Complexes](../../Complexes/package/Complexes.md)
- **Class:** [Symbol](../../Core/type/Symbol.md)
- **Aliases:** `Complexes$OverZZ`

## Description
Every module over the integers has projective dimension at most one.  This is the default strategy when the underlying ring is the integers, so in practice it never needs to be specified. Our first example is the cokernel of a $3 \times 3$ matrix with positive small integer entries. The next example shows that the projective dimension can be less than one.  In other words, a free module can have a non-trivial presentation. The final example involves a slightly larger matrix. The first matrix of the free resolution is the minimal presentation of the module.

name: POSIX
markdown: # POSIX Evaluate a regular expression search - **Package:** [Core](../../Core/package/Core.md) - **Class:** [Symbol](../../Core/type/Symbol.md) - **Aliases:** `Core$POSIX` ## Description The value returned is a list of pairs of integers corresponding to the parenthesized subexpressions successfully matched, suitable for use as the first argument of [substring](../../Core/function/substring.md). The first member of each pair is the offset within `str` of the substring matched, and the second is the length. See [regular expressions](regular_spc_expressions.md) for a brief introduction to the topic. By default, the regular expressions are interpreted using the Perl flavor, which supports features such as lookaheads and lookbehinds for fine-tuning the matches. This syntax is used in Perl and JavaScript languages. Alternatively, one can choose the POSIX Extended flavor of regex using `POSIX => true`. This syntax is similar to the one used by the Unix utilities `egrep` and `awk` and enforces the leftmost, longest rule for finding matches. If there's a tie, the rule is applied to the first subexpression. In the Perl flavor, one can specify whether repetitions should be possessive or non-greedy. ## Examples ```macaulay2 s = "The cat is black."; ``` ```macaulay2 m = regex("(\\w+) (\\w+) (\\w+)",s) ``` ``` o2 = {(0, 10), (0, 3), (4, 3), (8, 2)} o2 : List ``` ```macaulay2 substring(m#0, s) ``` ``` o3 = The cat is ``` ```macaulay2 substring(m#1, s) ``` ``` o4 = The ``` ```macaulay2 substring(m#2, s) ``` ``` o5 = cat ``` ```macaulay2 substring(m#3, s) ``` ``` o6 = is ``` ```macaulay2 s = "aa aaaa"; ``` ```macaulay2 m = regex("a+", 0, s) ``` ``` o8 = {(0, 2)} o8 : List ``` ```macaulay2 substring(m#0, s) ``` ``` o9 = aa ``` ```macaulay2 m = regex("a+", 2, s) ``` ``` o10 = {(7, 4)} o10 : List ``` ```macaulay2 substring(m#0, s) ``` ``` o11 = aaaa ``` ```macaulay2 m = regex("a+", 2, 3, s) ``` ```macaulay2 s = "line 1\nline 2\r\nline 3"; ``` ```macaulay2 m = regex("^.*$", 8, -8, s) ``` ``` o14 = {(7, 6)} o14 : List ``` ```macaulay2 substring(m#0, s) ``` ``` o15 = line 2 ``` ```macaulay2 m = regex("^", 10, -10, s) ``` ``` o16 = {(7, 0)} o16 : List ``` ```macaulay2 substring(0, m#0#0, s) ``` ``` o17 = line 1 ``` ```macaulay2 substring(m#0#0, s) ``` ``` o18 = line 2 line 3 ``` ```macaulay2 m = regex("^.*$", 4, -10, s) ``` ``` o19 = {(0, 6)} o19 : List ``` ```macaulay2 substring(m#0, s) ``` ``` o20 = line 1 ``` ```macaulay2 m = regex("a.*$", 4, -10, s) ``` ```macaulay2 regex("A(?!C)", "AC AB") ``` ``` o22 = {(3, 1)} o22 : List ``` ```macaulay2 regex("A(?=B)", "AC AB") ``` ``` o23 = {(3, 1)} o23 : List ``` ```macaulay2 s = "bold and strong"; ``` ```macaulay2 m = regex("(.*)", s, POSIX => true); ``` ```macaulay2 substring(m#1, s) ``` ``` o26 = bold and strong ``` ```macaulay2 m = regex("(.*?)", s); ``` ```macaulay2 substring(m#1, s) ``` ``` o28 = bold ``` ## Source ```m2 if opts.?POSIX and instance(opts.POSIX, Boolean) then if opts.POSIX ``` ## See also - [match](../../Core/methodFunction/match.md) - [regexQuote](../../Core/methodFunction/regexQuote.md) - [regular expressions](regular_spc_expressions.md) - [replace(String,String,String)](replace_lpar_String_cma_String_cma_String_rpar_.md) - [select(String,String,String)](select_lpar_String_cma_String_cma_String_rpar_.md) - [separate](../../Core/methodFunction/separate.md) - [strings and nets](strings_spc_and_spc_nets.md) - [substring](../../Core/function/substring.md)

# PackageCitations
A package facilitating citation of Macaulay2 packages

- **Package:** [PackageCitations](../../PackageCitations/package/PackageCitations.md)
- **Version:** 0.1
- **Class:** [Package](../../Core/type/Package.md)
- **Aliases:** `Package$PackageCitations`, `PackageCitations$PackageCitations`

## Description
This is a modest package with lofty goals. It is modest because it is a package for a powerful open-source mathematical software suite but it contains only one method and adds exactly zero computational ability to the platform. The one method, called [cite](../../PackageCitations/function/cite.md), can be called on any [Macaulay2](https://macaulay2.com/) package and will return a bibtex citation for inclusion in a [LaTeX](https://www.latex-project.org) document. For example, a citation for this package can be obtained as follows. The inner workings of [cite](../../PackageCitations/function/cite.md) are explained on the [cite](../../PackageCitations/function/cite.md) so we won't give any details here except to point out that the preferred citation for Macaulay2 can also be obtained with ease. The initial benefit of having a fast and facile mechanism for citing packages should be that more users of the software will include citations in their work. This, of course, will benefit the community in a number of ways. First it will recognize the hard work of the coders in the Macaulay2 community and second it will serve as valuable promotion for the platform and encourage new users and coders to join the community.### AuthorFor the programmerThe object [PackageCitations](../../PackageCitations/package/PackageCitations.md) is a [Package](../../Core/type/Package.md), defined in `PackageCitations.m2`.

## Authors
- Aaron Dall

```
"https://github.com/aarondall/PackageCitations-M2"}
```

name: ParallelizeByDegree
markdown:
# ParallelizeByDegree
Parallelism in engine computations

- **Package:** [Core](../../Core/package/Core.md)
- **Class:** [Symbol](../../Core/type/Symbol.md)
- **Aliases:** `Core$ParallelizeByDegree`

## Description
Some computations in the engine can run using multiple cores on your computer. Currently, this includes computation of minimal betti diagrams, non-minimal resolutions, and Gröbner bases of 2-sided ideals in associative algebras, all in the graded case, over a finite field.  Also included is (one of the algorithms for) the computation of Gröbner bases in polynomial rings over finite fields, whether graded or not. The variable `numTBBThreads` controls the number of cores used by Macaulay2. The default value (zero) means the system can choose an appropriate number of cores (often the maximum available).  Note that the default behavior is to use multiple cores. In [minimalBetti](../../Core/methodFunction/minimalBetti.md), and in [freeResolution](../../Complexes/methodFunction/freeResolution.md) with the `Strategy => Nonminimal` option, more aggressive parallelism that sometimes uses a lot of memory but can sometimes produce answers in less time can be enabled using the `ParallelizeByDegree` boolean option. For examples, we show some simple examples of computation which, for larger size problems, might benefit from using parallelism.  Note that in each of these cases, the default is to use all available CPU cores for computation. For these particularly simple examples, the overhead for using multiple cores is non-trivial with respect to the total computation time.  Significant speedup is achieved when the time to gauss reduce the requisite matrices is large compared to creating these matrices. Gröbner bases (based on a linear algebra method, e.g. Faugere's F4 algorithm, are also parallelized.  Note: the MGB Strategy of groebnerBasis is not currently parallelized. For Gröbner basis computation in associative algebras, `ParallelizeByDegree` is not relevant.  In this case, use `numTBBThreads` to control the amount of parallelism.

# PlaneCurveSingularities
Using the Rees Algebra to resolve plane curve singularities

- **Package:** [ReesAlgebra](../../ReesAlgebra/package/ReesAlgebra.md)
- **Class:** [Symbol](../../Core/type/Symbol.md)
- **Aliases:** `ReesAlgebra$PlaneCurveSingularities`
- **See also:** _undocumented_

## Description
The Rees Algebra of an ideal I appeared classically as the bihomogeneous coordinate ring of the blow up of the ideal I, used in resolution of singularities. Though the general case is still out of reach, we illustrate with some simple examples of plane curve singularities. First the cusp in the affine planeThe cusp is singular at the maximal ideal (x, y), so we blow that up, and examine the ``total transform'', that is, the ideal generated by the x^2-y^3 in the Rees algebra. Application of `first flattenRing` serves to make B a quotient of the polynomial ring T in 4 variables; otherwise it would be a quotient of R[w_0, w_1], which Macaulay2 treats as a polynomial ring in 2 variables, and the calculation of the singular locus later on would be wrong. We see that the reduced preimage consists of two codimension 1 components, the `exceptional divisor', which is the pullback of the point we blew up, (x, y), and the `strict transform'. The two components meet in a double point in the 2 dimensional variety B \subset{} A^2\times P^1. We have to saturate with respect to the irrelevant ideal to understand what's going on. We can see the multiplicities of these components by comparing their degrees to the degrees of the reduced componentsThat is, the exceptional component occurs with multiplicity 2 (in general we'd get the exceptional component with multiplicity equal to the multiplicity of the singular point we blew up.)We next investigate the singularity of the strict transform. We want to see it as a curve in P^1 x A^2, that is, as an ideal of  T = kk[w_0, w_1, x, y]We see that the singular locus of the strict transform is empty; that is, the curve is smooth. We could have made the computation in B as well: Next we look at the desingularization of a tacnode; it will take two blowups. Here proj1 mm is the ideal of the exceptional divisor. The strict transform is, by definition, obtained by saturating it away, The strict transform of the tacnode is not yet smooth: it consists of two smooth branches, meeting transversely at a point: We compute the singular point of the strict transform:...and blow up B1, getting a variety in P^2 x P^1 x A^2We compute the singular locus once again: The answer, `ideal 1` shows that the second blowup desingularizes the tacnode. It is not necessary to repeatedly blow up closed points: there is always a single ideal that can be blown up to desingularize (Hartshorne, Algebraic Geometry, Thm II.7.17). In this case, blowing-up (x, y^2) desingularizes the tacnode x^2-y^4 in a single step. So this single blowup is already nonsingular.

# Polyhedra
For computations with convex polyhedra, cones, and fans

- **Package:** [Polyhedra](../../Polyhedra/package/Polyhedra.md)
- **Version:** 1.10
- **Class:** [Package](../../Core/type/Package.md)
- **Aliases:** `Package$Polyhedra`, `Polyhedra$Polyhedra`
- **Examples:** _undocumented_
- **See also:** _undocumented_

## Description
A rational convex [Polyhedron](../../Polyhedra/type/Polyhedron.md) is the intersection of finitely many affine half-spaces over [QQ](../../Core/type/QQ.md) or equivalently, the convex hull of a finite set of vertices and rays. A rational convex polyhedral [Cone](../../Polyhedra/type/Cone.md) is the intersection of finitely many linear half-spaces over [QQ](../../Core/type/QQ.md) or equivalently, the positive hull of a finite set of rays. A [Fan](../../Polyhedra/type/Fan.md) is a finite collection of cones such that for each cone all its faces are in the fan and for two cones in the fan the intersection is a face of each.`Polyhedra` uses the [FourierMotzkin](FourierMotzkin.md) package by [Gregory G. Smith](http://www.mast.queensu.ca/~ggsmith)[FourTiTwo](FourTiTwo.md) package by [Michael Stillman](http://pi.math.cornell.edu/~mike/), [Josephine Yu](http://people.math.gatech.edu/~jyu67/), and [Sonja Petrovic](http://math.iit.edu/~spetrov1/)[Normaliz](Normaliz.md) package by Gesa Kaempf and Christof Soeger[Topcom](Topcom.md) package by [Michael Stillman](http://pi.math.cornell.edu/~mike/). Here are some examples illustrating the main uses of this package.[Working with polyhedra](Working_spc_with_spc_polyhedra.md)[Working with cones](Working_spc_with_spc_cones.md)[Working with fans](Working_spc_with_spc_fans.md)Please have a look at [V- and H-representation](V-_spc_and_spc_H-representation.md) on conventions used throughout this package before you start. For an introduction to polyhedra and cones, we recommend [Gunter M. Ziegler's](http://www.mi.fu-berlin.de/math/groups/discgeom/ziegler/) Lectures on Polytopes, Graduate Texts in Mathematics 152, Springer-Verlag, New York, 1995. The authors would like to thank [Daniel R. Grayson](https://faculty.math.illinois.edu/~dan/)[Nathan Ilten](http://people.cs.uchicago.edu/~nilten/)[Marta Panizzut](http://page.math.tu-berlin.de/~panizzut/)[Gregory G. Smith](http://www.mast.queensu.ca/~ggsmith/)[Andrew P. Staal](http://astaal.be/)[Michael Stillman](http://pi.math.cornell.edu/~mike/)[Anna-Lena Winz](http://www.mi.fu-berlin.de/math/groups/ag-algebra/members/mitarbeiter/Winz.html)for code contributions, bug reports, and helpful discussions concerning this package.### AuthorsFor the programmerThe object [Polyhedra](../../Polyhedra/package/Polyhedra.md) is a [Package](../../Core/type/Package.md), defined in `Polyhedra.m2`, with auxiliary files in `Polyhedra/`.

# PolyhedralComplex
The class of all polyhedral complexes

- **Package:** [Polyhedra](../../Polyhedra/package/Polyhedra.md)
- **Class:** [Type](../../Core/type/Type.md)
- **Parent:** [PolyhedralObject](../../Polyhedra/type/PolyhedralObject.md)
- **Aliases:** `Polyhedra$PolyhedralComplex`
- **See also:** _undocumented_

## Description
A PolyhedralComplex represents a complex of rational convex polyhedra, i.e. a collection of polyhedra, such that for every polyhedron in the complex all faces are in the complex and for every two polyhedra in the complex their intersection is a face of each (intersection condition). It need not be full dimensional or pure, and the polyhedra need not be compact. It is saved as a hash table which contains a list of the generating polyhedra of the complex starting with those of maximal dimension. So for every polyhedron in this list all faces are considered to be in the complex. The output of a PolyhedralComplex looks like this: This table displays a short summary of the properties of the PolyhedralComplex. However, one can not access the above information directly, because this is just a virtual hash table generated for the output. The data defining a PolyhedralComplex is extracted by the functions included in this package. A PolyhedralComplex can be constructed by collecting Polyhedra that satisfy the intersection condition. Every polyhedron that is added to a PolyhedralComplex is always considered as the collection of the Polyhedron and all of its faces.

- [HashTable](../../Core/type/HashTable.md)

# Polyhedron
The class of all convex polyhedra

- **Package:** [Polyhedra](../../Polyhedra/package/Polyhedra.md)
- **Class:** [Type](../../Core/type/Type.md)
- **Parent:** [PolyhedralObject](../../Polyhedra/type/PolyhedralObject.md)
- **Aliases:** `Polyhedra$Polyhedron`
- **See also:** _undocumented_

## Description
A Polyhedron represents a rational polyhedron. It can be bounded or unbounded, need not be full dimensional or may contain a proper affine subspace. It can be empty or zero dimensional. It is saved as a hash table which contains the vertices, generating rays, and the basis of the lineality space of the Polyhedron as well as the defining affine half-spaces and hyperplanes. The output of a Polyhedron looks like this: This table displays a short summary of the properties of the Polyhedron. Note that the number of rays and vertices are modulo the lineality space. So for example a line in QQ^2 has one vertex and no rays. However, one can not access the above information directly, because this is just a virtual hash table generated for the output. The data defining a Polyhedron is extracted by the functions included in this package. A Polyhedron can be constructed as the convex hull ([convexHull](../../Polyhedra/methodFunction/convexHull.md)) of a set of points and a set of rays or as the intersection ([polyhedronFromHData](../../Polyhedra/methodFunction/polyhedronFromHData.md)) of a set of affine half-spaces and affine hyperplanes. For example, consider the square and the square with an emerging ray for the convex hull: If we take the intersection of the half-spaces defined by the directions of the vertices and 1 we get the crosspolytope: This can for example be embedded in 3-space on height 1: See also [Working with polyhedra](Working_spc_with_spc_polyhedra.md).

## Ancestors
- [MutableHashTable](../../Core/type/MutableHashTable.md)
- [HashTable](../../Core/type/HashTable.md)
- [Thing](../../Core/type/Thing.md)

## Constructors
- [affineHull](../../Polyhedra/methodFunction/affineHull.md)

name: Position
markdown:
# Position
Monomial ordering

- **Package:** [Core](../../Core/package/Core.md)
- **Class:** [Symbol](../../Core/type/Symbol.md)
- **Aliases:** `Core$Position`

## Description
`MonomialOrder` -- an optional argument used with polynomial rings and monoids to indicate a monomial ordering other than the default (graded reverse lexicographic). In Macaulay2, each polynomial ring (and also each monoid) is equipped with a monomial order, which is used for display of polynomials (terms are listed in descending monomial order), and also for Gröbner basis computations. In the most general setting, a monomial ordering is given by a list of ordering tests, of various types listed and described below, each of which provides a partial ordering on the monomials.  The ordering tests are applied sequentially, starting with the first one, until one monomial is judged greater than the other. At the end, if necessary, the graded reverse lexicographic order is used to compare the monomials. For examples, see below, or see [monomial orderings](monomial_spc_orderings.md). Permissible elements:[GRevLex](../../Core/symbol/GRevLex.md) => n -- A graded reverse lexicographic block of variables[Lex](../../Core/symbol/Lex.md) => n[Weights](../../Core/symbol/Weights.md) => {...}[Position](../../Core/symbol/Position.md) => Up  or  Position => Down[RevLex](../../Core/symbol/RevLex.md) => n[GroupLex](../../Core/symbol/GroupLex.md) => n[GroupRevLex](../../Core/symbol/GroupRevLex.md) => n[MonomialSize](../../Core/symbol/MonomialSize.md) => n, n being 8,16,32, or 64.  Set the packing size for exponents for further variablesSome examples of monomial orders.  Note that if only one item is in the list, we can dispense with the list.`MonomialOrder => {GRevLex=>2, GRevLex=>3}` -- a product order`MonomialOrder => {2, 3}` -- same`MonomialOrder => {Weights=>{1,13,6,2}}` -- a weight order`MonomialOrder => Weights=>{1,13,6,2}` -- sameIf any monomials will be less than 1 in the ordering, then the option `Global => false` should be used.

## Examples
```macaulay2
QQ[x,y, Weights => {-1,1}, Global => false]
```

```
o1 = QQ[x..y]
o1 : PolynomialRing
```

```macaulay2
x<1
```

```
o2 = true
```

```macaulay2
y<1
```

```
o3 = false
```

## See also
- [grevlexWeight](grevlexWeight.md)
- [monomial orderings](monomial_spc_orderings.md)
- [weightGrevlex](weightGrevlex.md)

# Program
External program object

- **Package:** [Core](../../Core/package/Core.md)
- **Class:** [Type](../../Core/type/Type.md)
- **Parent:** [HashTable](../../Core/type/HashTable.md)
- **Aliases:** `Core$Program`
- **Examples:** _undocumented_

## Description
A hash table returned by [findProgram](../../Core/methodFunction/findProgram.md) with the following strings as keys:`"name"`, the name of the loaded program.  This comes from the first argument passed to [findProgram](../../Core/methodFunction/findProgram.md).  It is also what is displayed when printing a Program.`"path"`, the path to the program as determined by [findProgram](../../Core/methodFunction/findProgram.md).`"prefix"`, a sequence of two strings identifying the prefix prepended to the binary executables.  See [findProgram](../../Core/methodFunction/findProgram.md), specifically the description of the `Prefix` option, for more.`"version"`, a string containing the version number of the program. ## Description
The Macaulay2 interpreter compiles its language into pseudocode, which is evaluated later, step by step.  At each step, the evaluator is considering a pseudocode item.
